instructions:
You are the resilience analyst of an AI-driven chaos-engineering agent. The system under test is Google's Online
Boutique (11 gRPC microservices) on single-node Kubernetes. You get the measured facts of every experiment, the
dependency map, the baseline, the planner's predictions and how they held, anchor scores computed by code, and the
catalog of fixes.

Produce:
1. Findings = weaknesses, ranked by severity (most severe first). Severity scale: {"critical": "users cannot shop or check out (outage or most requests failing) and nothing contains it", "high": "a core flow (product, cart, checkout) breaks or becomes unusably slow (seconds), or recovery is slow", "medium": "noticeable degradation with a workaround or limited scope (one flow, moderate slowdown)", "low": "minor impact, or a configuration weakness without measured user impact yet"}.
   Each finding: affected services, the run ids that show it (exactly as given), the measured numbers, the root
   cause (explain the mechanism, e.g. sequential calls without deadlines amplify latency), ONE fix from the fix
   catalog with concrete parameters, why it addresses the root cause, the improvement you expect, and the
   experiment to re-run after the fix (same type/target/params as the evidence run when possible).
   Positive findings (e.g. graceful degradation) may be included as low severity with a code_change or posture fix
   only if useful; do not invent problems without evidence. Merge findings that share one root cause.
2. Resilience scores: for EVERY service in the anchors table, score each rubric dimension 0-100:
   {"availability": "Did users keep getting successful responses? 100 = no extra errors; 70 = a few % errors or short error bursts; 40 = sustained errors on some flows; 0 = most requests failed.", "latency": "How much slower did user flows get (worst p95 vs baseline)? 100 = < 1.5x; 80 = ~3x; 60 = ~10x; 30 = ~50x; 0 = several seconds / timeouts.", "recovery": "How fast were users back to normal after the fault ended? 100 = immediately or never impacted; 75 = ~30 s; 50 = ~60 s; 0 = not recovered within 180 s.", "containment": "Did the failure stay contained? 100 = callers degraded gracefully, no spread; lower when flows that depend on the service broke, when unrelated flows/pods were hit, or when the guard had to stop the experiment.", "posture": "Static resilience configuration: 100 = >= 2 replicas, readiness + liveness probes, CPU/memory limits; single replica -40, missing readiness -20, missing liveness -10, missing limits -20."}
   Start from the anchor and stay within +-15 of it; deviate only with a reason (e.g. impact
   on an optional feature like ads matters less; a slow recovery on the checkout path matters more). Untested
   services: score availability/latency/recovery/containment from posture and dependencies, close to the anchor
   (anchors for untested dimensions are null - use your judgement and say so). Choose a criticality weight per
   service (0.5-3) reflecting business impact (checkout path and entrypoint high, ads/recommendations low).
3. Explain how you weighed services, review how well the planner's predictions held, and list limitations
   (single VM, small probe, short experiments).
Use only facts you are given or fetch with the tools. Answer only with the structured report.

output.summary: Both experiments exposed checkoutservice as a single point of failure: checkout requests failed heavily during a sustained pod outage and during near-limit memory stress. The impact was confined to checkout, while the other measured flows remained error-free; the guard stopped both experiments after 6.6 seconds of fault exposure. Adding a second checkoutservice replica addresses the availability weakness, while increasing its memory limit addresses the separate restart observed under memory stress. All services are single-replica deployments, but only checkoutservice was exercised in these runs, so scores for the other services are posture- and dependency-based estimates.

findings.title: A single checkoutservice replica makes checkout unavailable during a pod outage
findings.evidence: Baseline checkout p95 was 21.6 ms with 0% errors. During the run, checkout had 87.5% errors (7/8 requests) and a p95 of 173.5 ms (8.03x baseline); the run-level impact error rate was 17.07%, with a 20% peak. The fault was active for 6.6 s before the 15% error guard aborted it; checkoutservice restarted twice and recovery was 4 s. Home, product, add_to_cart, and view_cart each had 0% errors.
findings.root_cause: checkoutservice has one replica and is the sole service handling the checkout RPC path. When that pod is unavailable, frontend checkout calls have no alternate instance, so checkout fails even though unrelated flows remain available.
findings.fix_rationale: A second stateless checkoutservice replica provides an alternate instance if one pod becomes unavailable, addressing the single point of failure shown by the pod-failure run.
findings.expected_improvement: On rerun, a failure affecting one replica should no longer cause most checkout requests to fail; checkout error rate should fall substantially and ideally remain below the 15% guard, with less checkout latency impact. Other flows should remain unaffected.

findings.title: Near-limit memory stress restarts the only checkoutservice pod and interrupts checkout
findings.evidence: checkoutservice had a 128 Mi memory limit. With 124 MB stress allocation and one worker, checkout had 100% errors (12/12 requests), one checkoutservice restart, and 9 s recovery; the fault was active for 6.6 s before the 15% error guard aborted it. Run-level impact error rate was 19.35%, with a 21% peak. The reported checkout p95 was 2.5 ms, but this was alongside 100% checkout errors and is not evidence of successful low-latency checkout. Other measured flows had 0% errors.
findings.root_cause: The stress allocation was close to the pod's 128 Mi memory limit and coincided with a restart. Because checkoutservice has only one replica, that restart removed all checkout capacity for the interval. The run supports a memory-headroom weakness, though it does not independently confirm the exact termination reason.
findings.fix_rationale: Raising the memory limit from 128 Mi to 256 Mi gives the service additional headroom for the tested allocation, reducing the likelihood that near-limit memory use restarts the pod. The CPU limit stays at its current 200m because these runs did not indicate CPU pressure.
findings.expected_improvement: With the same 124 MB stress, checkoutservice should avoid a memory-related restart and checkout errors should decrease substantially; the other flows should remain unaffected.

output.score_explanation: All services have one replica, readiness and liveness probes, and CPU and memory limits, giving a posture score of 60 under the stated rubric. For untested impact dimensions, scores are kept at 60 because the experiments provide no service-specific evidence to justify further deviation; dependency reach and business role are reflected primarily in criticality weights. checkoutservice scores reflect its measured checkout errors, 8.03x worst flow p95 in the pod-failure run, short 4–9 s recovery, and the fact that other measured flows stayed error-free. Weights are capped at 3.0: the entrypoint, cart and product/catalog paths, and checkout-critical services receive higher weight, while optional or limited-reach services such as ads and recommendations receive lower weight.
output.planner_review: The planner correctly identified checkout as the affected flow and predicted that both experiments would abort; both runs did abort after the error guard was breached. For pod failure, its error-band prediction was recorded as a miss, even though the observed checkout flow had 87.5% errors and the run reached a 20% peak error rate; the planner also missed the observed slowdown. For memory stress, it correctly predicted high errors and the affected flow, but predicted moderate slowdown when the reported p95 did not show one; that p95 coincided with 100% checkout errors. Overall, predictions captured the scope and guarded outcome, but were inconsistent on the severity and latency signals.
limitations: The system runs on a single-node Kubernetes environment, so results do not establish resilience to node or cluster failure.
Only checkoutservice was targeted; other service scores' impact dimensions are estimates based on posture and dependencies, not measured resilience.
Experiments were short, and the guard stopped each fault after 6.6 seconds, limiting evidence about longer outages and sustained recovery.
Checkout flow samples were small (8 requests in the pod-failure run and 12 in the memory-stress run); percentages and p95 values are therefore sensitive to individual requests.
The memory-stress run showed a restart during near-limit allocation, but the supplied measurements do not independently establish the precise termination cause.
